To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cumulative daily average fluoride intakes in children are higher than the tolerable intake limit when the maximum exposures to fluoride from all exposure pathways are considered.
children living in areas where municipal water supplies are fluoridated are exposed to higher levels of fluoride than those living in non-fluorinated areas.

the estimated average daily intake of total fluoride via all applicable pathways contributing to fluoridosis risk for infants living in fluoridated communities was 0.20 mg/kg-day for the RME scenario and 0.10 mg/kg-day for CTE scenario.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a mathematical model to estimate the risk of fluorosis from exposure to fluoride through all applicable exposure pathways.
the risk of developing dental fluorosis in children.
the development of an integrated risk assessment approach that can be applied to the assessment of fluoride exposure and intake in children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk of dental fluorosis is low for infants and children in fluoridated communities.
the risk of dental fluorosis is low for infants and children in fluoridated and unfluoridated areas, but it cannot be completely ruled out.
children living in fluoridated and/or non-fluorinated communities are at risk for dental fluorosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the RME estimates are above the optimum level for dental caries protection and below the level for fluorosis.
children living in fluoridated communities are at greater risk for fluorosis than children living in non-fluoride communities.
children in the United States are exposed to fluoride from multiple pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a mathematical model that is used for health risk assessment of chemicals in the environment can be used to estimate fluoride exposure and risk for children.
the current practice of water fluoridation is not a risk-free practice.
the risk assessment framework can be a useful tool to identify exposure pathways and sources that are contributing to excessive fluoride intake and, therefore, to fluorosis risk.
